article.text:
Back to changelog
Release
October 28, 2026 •
2 minute read
GitHub Copilot app, Universe releases
Work doesn’t always fit in a single repository or session. A feature can span several repositories. A launch plan can pull in specs, designs, and assets without touching a repository at all. Projects in the GitHub Copilot app give that work one home, with its context, agents, and results together. Copilot coordinates the work in the background and checks in when it needs you.
Give Copilot a goal
Start a project, describe what you want to get done, and add the context Copilot needs (e.g., repositories, design mocks, Slack threads, or notes from a design meeting). Choose the models and tools for the job. Copilot runs as many agents as the work needs and brings back results (e.g., pull requests) for your review.
Use project automations for repeatable tasks, such as creating a new promo video whenever a feature lands.
For a focused task in a single repository, you can still start a session directly from that repository.
Copilot Projects are now in public preview. You can learn more in the projects documentation.
Handle the work around your code
Use context from connected tools such as Slack and Figma to research a request, draft a specification, or work through a design alongside your code.
You can also generate and edit images using natural language in chat.
Let Copilot work with your desktop apps
Ask Copilot to work through tasks in your desktop apps, such as an expense-report workflow. Computer use—in public preview on macOS and Windows—lets Copilot read app content, click controls, enter or edit text, and navigate across apps, including those without an API, command-line interface, or MCP integration.
Copilot asks for your approval before controlling an app, and your organization can disable the feature through managed settings. To get started, open Settings > Computer Use and turn on Enable Computer Use. On macOS, grant the required Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions.
For more information, see the computer use documentation.
Get started
Download or update the GitHub Copilot app and join the discussion in GitHub Community.

article.title: Changelog | Google Antigravity Docs
article.text:
v2.29.0
Latest
November 3, 2026
Voice mode, remote agents, redesigned Automations, and Jupyter notebook viewer
Voice mode, enabled by Gemini Live, and remote agents, which run conversations in the cloud, are starting to roll out. This release also adds redesigned Home and Automations pages, a native Jupyter notebook viewer, and downloads and browsing history in the built-in browser.
Improvements(22)
Voice mode, enabled by Gemini Live, lets you talk to Antigravity and hand requests to the agent by voice. Start it from the button in an empty message box. Voice mode is rolling out gradually, so you may not see it yet.
Remote agents are starting to roll out to Google AI Ultra and Pro subscribers. Conversations in a cloud project run in the cloud instead of on your computer, and you can also open them at antigravity.google.com/remote.
The new-conversation page now greets you at the top and pins the message box to the bottom. Single-repo projects combine branch and Git worktree selection into one menu, and the agent picker now lives inside the model menu.
The Automations page now organizes automations into Scheduled, Always on, and Paused lists with Next run and Last run times, plain-menu schedule pickers, in-page details, and a full-page creation form.
Jupyter notebook .ipynb files now open natively in the file viewer, rendering code cells, Markdown, tables, images, and cell outputs without leaving Antigravity.
Long conversations in the conversation navigator now label each collapsed chapter card with a short AI-generated title instead of only a date.
The built-in browser now saves downloads directly to your downloads folder without blocking prompts, shows progress in a toolbar downloads drawer, and lets you choose a default download folder under Settings > General.
Typing in the built-in browser's address bar now suggests matching pages from your browsing history, and you can clear saved history under Settings > General.
The built-in browser has a redesigned address bar with clearer connection security indicators, a thin loading progress bar along the top of the page, and an in-page prompt dialog when a site asks for text input.
You can now open a web address or search Google from the side panel's New Tab page, drag links into the side panel to open them in the built-in browser, and close tabs to the left from a tab's menu.
Settings > Appearance now includes a Fill option that expands conversations to the full width of the center pane, a Font menu to switch between System UI, Inter, and Google Sans, and a Screen Reader Mode toggle under Accessibility.
If you haven't picked your own, Antigravity now uses the Onyx theme and the Google Sans font. You can change both under Settings > Appearance.
You can now customize keyboard shortcuts in Settings > Shortcuts, and reset any of them to the default.
Code blocks and diffs now load syntax highlighting on demand across 173 languages, and the file tree and tabs include file icons for more than 30 additional languages and config formats.
The Overview panel's Review row and the Review tab header now show total added and deleted line counts across changed files in your Git repository.
Opening antigravity:// links can now jump directly to a plugin or skill in the Marketplace, or open a new conversation with the prompt filled in for you to review and send.
The Git branch menu now adds a search box when a repository has more than 15 branches, refreshes automatically when you return to the window, and shows the checked-out commit hash when in detached HEAD state.
Agent question cards can now be collapsed while you read earlier messages and are automatically canceled if you send a new reply instead, and each permission preset in the message box now has its own icon.
In conversation search, you can now unarchive an archived conversation directly from its row, and the Automations filter includes archived automation runs.
Opening an image from a Markdown carousel now lets you step through every slide…

Boris from the Claude Code team here. Historically Claude Code has not done secret scrubbing (there are many good tools for that), but we are looking into what we can do to prevent this.
That said, a few thoughts:
1. .claude/settings.local.json is meant to stay local. This is not a file you should check into source control. We automatically gitignore it when Claude creates the file, so in this case the files were manually created and checked in (docs:…

comments.author: Aurornis
comments.text:
Confusing headline. They scanned for repos where people had committed their .claude/ folder and local settings and then scanned those files for commands which contained keys or passwords.
So pressing “Don’t Ask Again” by itself doesn’t expose passwords by itself. If you commit your local Claude settings and in those settings you have manually approved commands containing secrets directly in the command and then you publish the repo, that’s exposed.

Today, we’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, and making it generally available across the Gemini API and Gemini for business. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash introduces native 15-second video creation, multi-turn conversational editing capabilities, and enhanced reference following. We have dropped the price 30% from Gemini Omni 1.1 making it available at $0.07 per second for 720p video.
Here’s an overview of what’s new:
Fast and cost-effective at scale
Beyond the lower price, the workflow keeps costs down: you can draft fast at 360p or 720p, fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of re-generating the entire clip, and then upscale your best creations to 1080p or 4K.
Longer clips up to 15 seconds
You can now generate and edit videos natively up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1. You can also specify duration in one-second increments from 3 to 15 seconds, giving you room to tell complete stories, create product explainers, or produce full social ad spots in a single generation.
Better reference adherence
You can guide generation combining character, product, or style images, short motion clips (up to three seconds), and audio cues — and Omni 1.2 Flash holds onto those details from start to finish. Faces, garments, packaging typography, and brand colors stay consistent across camera angles, making it easy to turn existing product photography or character sheets into virtual try-on clips, catalog spins, and branded video ads.
Combining one model photo with front-and-back product shots of three outfits, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates a 15-second virtual try-on sequence across 360-degree turns and match cuts while keeping the model’s identity and each garment’s cut, drape, and back details consistent.
More consistent results
You can maintain stronger character, object, and scene consistency from the first to the last frame, with less visual drift or morphing across motion and camera transitions. Whether you’re interpolating between a first and last keyframe, or extending a clip to build a longer sequence, products, characters, props, and environments stay consistent from shot to shot.
Given the same static studio lighting exhibition poster and five-layer animation prompt, Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash does not match the reference image as closely as 1.2 does.
